questions.question_text: Mr. Liam Gideon is a 43-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with Huntington's disease after starting to exhibit characteristic movement abnormalities and subtle cognitive and mood changes. Which of the following is characteristic of the pathology of Huntington's disease?

options.text: Neuronal loss in the substantia nigra
Neuronal loss and gliosis in the caudate nucleus and the putamen

correct_answer.text: Neuronal loss and gliosis in the caudate nucleus and the putamen

correct_answers.text: Neuronal loss and gliosis in the caudate nucleus and the putamen

questions.explanation: Early neuronal loss in the caudate and putamen of the basal ganglia along with associated gliosis are characteristic of Huntington's disease. Neuronal loss in the substantia nigra is more characteristic of Parkinson's disease but can occur in Huntington's disease. Atrophy seen in Huntington's does not spare the hippocampus and eventually results in ventriculomegaly. Astrocytosis usually occurs but this is non-specific and is a response to neuronal loss regardless of cause.

questions.question_text: Which of the following brain regions, when impaired in its function, severely limits empathetic expression during social judgments?
questions.explanation: 1) Delirium tremens, unlike other delirium states which are characterised by diffuse slowing of background rhythms to alpha, theta and finally delta waves, tends to show excessive but low voltage fast wave, or beta, activity of 13-30Hz. 2) Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is associated with characteristic 4-6Hz polyspike and wave discharges. Other abnormalities can also be seen, including generalized single spike waves. 3) In typical absence seizures the ictal EEG shows a characteristic regular and symmetrical generalised discharges of 3-4 Hz "spike and slow" wave complexes, and may also have multiple spike and slow wave complexes. 4) West Syndrome, or infantile spasms, is a severe form of epilepsy, usually presenting in early adulthood, which is associated with hypsarrhythmia on EEG, which is chaotic, high amplitude slow, sharp and poly-spike waves. Ref: Britton JW, Frey LC, Hopp JLet al., authors; St. Louis EK, Frey LC, editors. Electroencephalography (EEG): An Introductory Text and Atlas of Normal and Abnormal Findings in Adults, Children, and Infants [Internet]. Chicago: American Epilepsy Society; 2016. EEG in the Epilepsies. Available from: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK390347/

questions.explanation: The locus coeruleus is a small nucleus in the dorsal pons comprising the main source of noradrenaline in the brain via its diffuse projections. It has projections through the brain and into the spinal cord.

questions.question_text: Anti-NMDA encephalitis is an autoimmune disease causing inflammation of the brain associated with acute psychotic symptoms. Which class of immunoglobulin in the CSF should be tested when suspecting anti-NMDA encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Damage to the left angular gyrus is associated with alexia and Gerstmann syndrome, characterised by dysgraphia/agraphia, dyscalculia/acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation.

questions.question_text: Which area of the brain is affected first in terms of atrophy (volume loss) seen in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: NMDAR antibody test is most sensitive and specific with CSF. Serum test for NMDAR antibody has a low false positive rate but a higher false negative rate. Pathogenic NMDAR autoantibodies are IgG responses. Both IgM and IgA responses are non-specific and are seen in patients with schizophrenia and other psychiatric disease as well as ~10% of normal controls. As a result, we cannot use the IgM and IgA responses for diagnosing autoimmune encephalitis. Serum or CSF testing for IgG antibodies against the NR1a subunit of the NMDA receptor is typically performed when autoimmune encephalitis is suspected. NMDAR IgG responses seen in anti-NMDAR encephalitis are not seen in schizophrenia. Ref: Lancaster E. The diagnosis and treatment of autoimmune encephalitis. Journal of Clinical Neurology. 2016 Jan 1;12(1):13.

questions.question_text: Orexin (or hypocretin) is a hormone produced in the hypothalamus and is associated with a variety of bodily functions. Which of the following conditions is most associated with low levels or orexin?
questions.explanation: MRI studies have demonstrated that the entorhinal cortex is affected first in Alzheimer's disease. It is an area of the brain located in the medial temporal lobe and functions as the main interface between the hippocampus and neocortex. (Ref: Khan UA, Liu L, Provenzano FA, Berman DE, Profaci CP, Sloan R, Mayeux R, Duff KE, Small SA (2013). Molecular drivers and cortical spread of lateral entorhinal cortex dysfunction in preclinical Alzheimer's disease. Nature Neuroscience. 17: 304-311. doi:10.1038/nn.3606. PMC 4044925. PMID 24362760)

Low levels of orexin have been associated with feelings of sadness, while high levels are associated with happiness. High levels of orexin have been associated with increased appetite, adipose storage and addiction behaviours in animal studies.

questions.explanation: Low levels of CSF 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindole-acetic acid) have been consistently identified as being associated with aggressive and impulsive behaviour across a variety of studies and cultures.

questions.explanation: The mesolimbic dopamine pathway dysfunction is associated with positive symptoms, whereas the mesocortical dysfunction is associated with negative symptoms. It is important to note that this is a simplistic reduction that does not hold true in experimental models.

questions.explanation: A Southern blot is a method used in molecular biology for detection of a specific DNA sequence in DNA samples. Northern blot is for RNA, Western for proteins, Eastern for post-translational modifications (including the addition of lipids, phosphates, and glycoconjugates), Southwestern for DNA-binding proteins, and Northwestern is a hybrid method for detecting interactions between RNA and proteins.

questions.question_text: Parkinson's disease is associated with particular pathological changes within the brain, giving rise to the characteristic movement abnormalities and later cognitive changes. In which of the following areas of the brain are Lewy Bodies most commonly found in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Sleep studies in PTSD have been somewhat equivocal, although a meta-analysis of polysomnographic studies conducted with military veterans and civilian adults with PTSD found modest indices of objective sleep disruption in PTSD, as indicated by more stage 1 sleep, less slow-wave sleep and greater REM density than in subjects without PTSD. (Ref: Kobayashi I, Boarts JM, Delahanty DL. Polysomnographically measured sleep abnormalities in PTSD: a meta-analytic review. Psychophysiology. 2007;44:660-669).

questions.question_text: Mr. Alan Bradley is a 66-year-old man who has been admitted with a sudden onset of quadriplegia and incontinence after a head injury. He is unable to speak but can communicate by blinking. Which of the following brain areas is most likely to be damaged?
questions.explanation: Lewy Bodies are most prominent in the substantia nigra in Parkinson's disease. The main pathological characteristics of Parkinson's disease are cell death in the brain's basal ganglia (affecting up to 70% of the dopamine secreting neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta by the end of life) and the presence of Lewy bodies in many of the remaining neurons. This loss of neurons is accompanied by the death of astrocytes and a significant increase in the number of microglia in the substantia nigra.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Eva Clark is a 72-year-old woman who has experienced a stroke affecting her dominant parietal lobe. Which of the following is she most likely to experience as a result?
questions.explanation: This describes locked-in syndrome which can be classified into 3 categories: in the classic form patients are quadriplegic and anarthric with preserved consciousness and upper eyelid and vertical eye movements; in the incomplete form, patients still have limited voluntary movements other than vertical eye movements, most frequently of fingers, toes and head; in the total form, patients show complete immobility including eye movements but have preserved consciousness. It is usually due to traumatic or vascular damage to the brain stem, vertebral or basilar artery damage or occlusion, or compression of the cerebral peduncles from tentorial herniation. It is most often caused by damage to a specific part of the brainstem known as the pons. In locked-in syndrome there is an interruption of all the motor fibers running from grey matter in the brain via the spinal cord to the body's muscles and also damage to the centers in the brainstem important for facial control and speaking. Ref: Laureys S, et al. The locked-in syndrome: what is it like to be conscious but paralyzed and voiceless?. Progress in brain research. 2005 Jan 1;150:495-611.

questions.explanation: Damage to the dominant parietal lobe is likely to lead to: dysphasia/aphasia, dyscalculia, dyslexia, apraxia, tactile agnosia and Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia and right-left disorientation). The other options presented are more likely to occur if the non- dominant parietal lobe is damaged.

questions.explanation: Accumulation of amyloid ẞ-peptide (AB) is the main source of neuronal degeneration in Alzheimer's disease (AD). When ẞ-amyloid precursor protein (APP) is sequentially cleaved by ẞ- and y-secretase enzymes, this results in Aẞ (amyloidogenic pathway). When a-secretase acts on APP, this precludes Aẞ formation (non-amyloidogenic pathway). Reelin is a separate protein, which may interact with APP to have a role in Alzheimer's disease. Acetylcholinesterase is not a APP enzyme.

During this stage, individuals compare themselves more with their peers and may place emphasis on external validation to demonstrate their abilities.

questions.explanation: The mesolimbic pathway is sometimes referred to as the reward pathway. It connects the ventral tegmental area in the midbrain, to the ventral striatum of the basal ganglia in the forebrain. The ventral striatum includes the nucleus accumbens and the olfactory tubercle. The release of dopamine from the mesolimbic pathway into the nucleus accumbens regulates incentive salience (i.e. motivation and desire for rewarding stimuli) and facilitates reinforcement and reward-related motor function learning; it may also play a role in the subjective perception of pleasure.

questions.question_text: Normal aging is associated with a reduction in brain size, even in the absence of marked cognitive decline. Which of the following nuclei is least likely to degenerate in old age?
questions.explanation: Procedural memory is not based on the conscious recall of information, but on implicit learning. It can best be summarized as remembering how to do something, such as driving a car.

questions.question_text: Neuronal functioning relies upon a number of molecules, which can be divided into primary and secondary messengers. Which of the following acts as a second messenger in the Central Nervous System?
questions.explanation: Aging results in progressive loss of neuronal cell bodies in many regions of the brain and spinal cord. Motor neuron loss in the spinal cord leads to sarcopenia - a progressive age-related reduction in muscle mass. Cranial nerve nuclei withstand age-related degenerative changes to a large extent, though dendritic loss has been documented in several nuclei. Ref: Schwarz EC et al. The effects of aging on hypoglossal motoneurons in rats. Dysphagia. 2009 Mar 1;24(1):40.

questions.question_text: There are several important proteolytic enzymes in the brain that influence the development of certain neurological conditions. Which of the following enzymes preclude amyloid formation?
questions.explanation: Second messengers are intracellular signaling molecules released by the cell in response to exposure to extracellular signaling molecules- the first messengers. Second messengers trigger physiological changes at cellular level such as proliferation, differentiation, migration, survival, and apoptosis. Examples of second messenger molecules include cyclic AMP, cyclic GMP, inositol trisphosphate, diacylglycerol, and calcium. First messengers are extracellular factors, often hormones or neurotransmitters, such as adrenaline, growth hormone, and serotonin.

questions.question_text: Prions are misfolded proteins with the ability to transmit their misfolded shape onto normal variants of the same protein. They characterise several fatal and transmissible neurodegenerative diseases in humans and many other animals. Which part of the brain is most associated with prion diseases?
questions.explanation: Excess amyloid ẞ-peptide (AB) contributes to the neuronal degeneration in Alzheimer's disease. Aẞ is a 38-43 amino acid peptide derived from the ẞ-amyloid precursor protein (APP) through sequential cleavages by beta- and gamma-secretase enzymes. The cleavage site for another APP processing enzyme, alpha-secretase lies within the Aẞ sequence. Thus, the action of alpha secretase leads to non- amyloidogenic products and precludes Aẞ formation. Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2889200/

questions.question_text: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological condition characterised by certain motor symptoms, including tremor. Which of the following is true regarding the type of tremor seen in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: While prion diseases have a variety of clinical presentations, early symptoms generally include prominent cerebellar symptoms. As the disease progresses, patients generally develop global neurological symptoms. Mutations related to Prion diseases can result in different regions of the brain being affected. For example, thalamus is affected preferentially in fatal familial insomnia. While the cellular mechanisms involved in targeting specific neuronal populations and neuron-to-neuron spreading of prions in the CNS remain elusive, in several prion diseases, the cerebellum is a preferential prion target (Ref: Ragagnin A, et al. Prion Proteins and Neuronal Death in the Cerebellum. In Prions-Some Physiological and Pathophysiological Aspects 2018 Nov 5. Intech Open).

questions.explanation: The tremor associated with Parkinson's disease is present at rest, usually starts on one side of the body, has a frequency of 4-6Hz and is relatively low amplitude. Intention tremor is less common in Parkinson's disease than in essential tremor, but can occur. Ref; Thenganatt MA, Louis ED. Distinguishing essential tremor from Parkinson's disease: bedside tests and laboratory evaluations. Expert review of neurotherapeutics. 2012 Jun 1;12(6):687-96.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diseases is Progranulin associated with?
questions.explanation: Tau proteins aid in the stabilisation of microtubules when they are functioning normally. They are present in higher concentrations in neurons and are coded on chromosome 17 by MAPT (microtubule-associated protein tau). Tau proteins interact with tubulin to stabilize microtubules and promote tubulin assembly into microtubules. Tau has two ways of controlling microtubule stability: isoforms and phosphorylation. Hyperphosphorylation results in Tau becoming dysfunctional and accumulating, leading to neuronal degeneration. Ref: Kadavath et al. Tau stabilizes microtubules by binding at the interface between tubulin heterodimers. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2015 Jun 16;112(24):7501-6.

questions.question_text: Mr Gregory Perry is a 24 year old who is taken to A&E by his family after developing gradually increasing disorientation and confusion over several weeks and is now presenting with aggression and ill-formed delusions about people harming him. Due to him having some soft neurological symptoms, he is tested for autoimmune encephalitis. If this was the diagnosis, which of the following immunoglobulins would be most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia is familial in 25% - 50% of cases (autosomal dominant with high penetrance). Genes causing this type of FTD include MAPT, the gene encoding tau, CHMP2B, and GRN, the gene that encodes progranulin. GRN mutation results in ubiquitinated TAR DNA binding protein (TARDBP or TDP-43) deposits while tau tangles are rare. Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2901991/

questions.question_text: Mr Andrews Martins is a 45-year-old man who has been involved in a major motorcycle accident leaving him with residual cognitive changes. The neuropsychologist working with him is concerned about his executive function. Which of the following tests would be the appropriate to test his executive function?
questions.explanation: Autoantibody testing is extremely important for the proper diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis. Psychiatric manifestations are common early in the course of autoimmune encephalitis. These may include psychosis, aggression, inappropriate sexual behaviors, panic attacks, compulsive behaviors, euphoria or fear. Symptoms may fluctuate rapidly. Although this presentation is well known for anti-NMDAR encephalitis, anti-AMPAR and anti-GABA-B-R are also reported.. NMDAR and other cell surface antibody tests are most sensitive and specific with CSF. Serum may offer a low false positive rate and a higher false negative rate. Pathogenic cell surface or synaptic autoantibodies are IgG responses. NMDAR IgM and IgA responses have been reported in patients with schizophrenia and other psychiatric disease but also in up to 10% of normal controls; these IgM and IgA responses have no established role in diagnosing autoimmune encephalitis. (Ref: Lancaster E. The Diagnosis and Treatment of Autoimmune Encephalitis. J Clin Neurol. 2016;12(1):1-13. doi:10.3988/jcn.2016.12.1.1)

questions.question_text: Mrs. Jane Simons is a 45-year-old woman who develops gradual onset low mood and cognitive slowing which is followed by gait disturbance, in-coordination and then abnormal movements. She is later diagnosed with Huntington's disease and she and her family undergo genetic counselling. Which of the following chromosomes is affected in Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: The Tower of London test is a test used in applied clinical neuropsychology for the assessment of executive functioning specifically to detect deficits in planning.

questions.question_text: The amygdalae are almond-shaped clusters of nuclei located deep and medially within the temporal lobes of the brain and are considered part of the limbic system. Which of the following is a primary function of the amygdala?
questions.explanation: The Huntington gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 4. It contains a CAG trinucleotide repeat and if this exceeds 36 repeats, the individual is at risk of developing Huntington's disease, with penetrance being complete if there are 40 repeats or more.

questions.question_text: Suicide prevention is an increasingly important area of academic study. Which of the following neurochemical abnormalities is associated with an increased risk of suicide?
questions.explanation: The amygdalae have been shown to perform a primary role in the processing of memory, decision-making and emotional responses. They appear to regulate memory consolidation in other brain regions. During the consolidation period, the memory can be modulated. In particular, it appears that emotional arousal following the learning event influences the strength of the subsequent memory for that event. Greater emotional arousal following a learning event enhances a person's retention of that event. Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15217324

questions.question_text: Metabotropic receptors are indirectly linked to ion channels via signal transduction mechanisms, such as G-proteins. Which of the following is a metabotropic receptor?
questions.explanation: Reduced 5-HIAA levels (5-hydroxy indole acetic acid) in the CSF have been associated with aggression and suicide by violent means. They are thought to be related to reduced serotonin levels in the brain, as 5-HIAA is a metabolite of serotonin. Ref: Mehlman PT, et al. Low CSF 5-HIAA concentrations and severe aggression and impaired impulse control in nonhuman primates. The American journal of psychiatry. 1994 Oct.

questions.question_text: Cocaine is a common drug of abuse that has significant addictive potential. Which of the following brain areas is particularly affected by cocaine?
questions.explanation: Metabotropic receptors include muscarinic acetylcholine, metabotropic glutamate, GABA-B receptors as well as most serotonin receptors. The endocannabinoid $CB(1)$ or $CB(2)$ receptors are also metabotropic, though the endocannabinoids anandamide has been observed to have activating properties at certain voltage gated calcium ion channels. Ref; Di Marzo V. New approaches and challenges to targeting the endocannabinoid system. Nature Reviews Drug Discovery. 2018 Sep;17(9):623-39.

questions.question_text: Miss Charlotte Rankin is a 25-year-old woman who has to attend an alcohol awareness course after being convicted of drink-driving. Cocaine activates numerous areas within the brain during acute use, particularly within the limbic system.

questions.question_text: The dementias all have characteristic pathological changes on macroscopic and microscopic examination of brain tissue. Which of the following is characterised by microscopic spherical bodies?
questions.explanation: The enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase activity is a major rate limiting factor for ethanol metabolism in humans; as a result, excess consumption of alcohol induces zero order kinetics wherein only a fixed amount of alcohol gets oxidised. Ref: Jones AW. Alcohol, its absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion in the body and pharmacokinetic calculations. Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Forensic Science. 2019 Sep;1(5):e1340.

questions.question_text: Emma George is a 26-year-old woman who is experiencing repeated night mares. In which of the following stages of sleep are nightmares most likely to occur?
questions.explanation: Pick bodies are the characteristic morphology assumed by tau filaments in Pick's disease, in which they accumulate in limbic (especially hippocampal dentate gyrus) and cortical neurons. They are intraneuronal, approximately the size of the nucleus and are formed of disorganized bundles of filaments comprised of three 3-repeat isoforms of tau. questions.question_text: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a novel treatment in which a changing magnetic field is used to cause electric current at a specific area of the brain through electromagnetic induction. It has been studied in a variety of neurological and psychiatric conditions. Which of the following lobes of the brain is targeted when it is used in treatment resistant depression?
questions.explanation: Nightmares occur in REM sleep.

questions.question_text: Visualising specific tracts in the brain is useful in research and certain clinical circumstances. Which of the following is the best imaging technique for identifying a tract specific lesion?
questions.explanation: For treatment-resistant major depressive disorder, targeting of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) appears effective and low- frequency (LF) rTMS of the right DLPFC has probable efficacy. The most promising areas to target for OCD appear to be the orbitofrontal cortex.

questions.question_text: The pituitary gland, or hypophysis, is an endocrine gland about the size of a pea. It is a protrusion off the bottom of the hypothalamus at the base of the brain. It produces numerous hormones which influence a wide variety of bodily processes. Which of the following hormones are not synthesised in the pituitary?
questions.explanation: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is a magnetic resonance imaging technique that enables the measurement of the restricted diffusion of water in tissue in order to produce neural tract images instead of using this data solely for the purpose of assigning contrast or colors to pixels in a cross sectional image. The principal direction of the diffusion tensor can be used to infer the white matter connectivity of the brain. (This process is called tractography). For example, see Palaniyappan L, et al. Neuropsychopharmacology. 2013 Aug;38(9):1808.

questions.question_text: Mr Lawrence Graves is a 75 year old man with a diagnosis of probable Alzheimer's disease which is currently mild in severity. He is wondering about what is happening in his brain to cause his memory impairment. Which of the following is thought to be the earliest histological change in Alzheimer disease?
questions.explanation: Leptin is generally produced in the adipose tissue and enterocytes of the small intestine. The anterior pituitary produces: growth hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), beta-endorphin, melanocyte-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and prolactin. The intermediate lobe produces melanocyte-stimulating hormone. The posterior pituitary produces: vasopressin (anti-diuretic hormone) and oxytocin. Ref; Harris RB. Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA)-Molecular Basis of Disease. 2014 Mar 1;1842(3):414-23.

questions.question_text: Schizophrenia is a major research topic within psychiatry, in terms of causation, treatment and prognosis. Which of the following is a recent focus of genetic research in schizophrenia that is associated with intellectual deficits?
