It increases blood sugar through gluconeogenesis, suppresses the immune system, and aids in the metabolism of fat, protein, and carbohydrates. From which of the following areas is it secreted?
questions.explanation: A copy number variation (CNV) is when the number of copies of a particular gene varies from one individual to the next. They are recognised as contributing to both to normal genomic variability and risk for human diseases. Recent genome-wide studies have provided initial evidence that CNVs may also be associated with schizophrenia, especially in syndromes associated with intellectual deficits such as the Velocardiofacial Syndrome. Ref: Hiroi N, et al. Molecular psychiatry. 2013 Nov; 18(11):1153.

questions.question_text: Leptin is a hormone that has a role in satiety and the development of obesity. From which of the following areas is it secreted?
questions.explanation: Cortisol is a steroid hormone, in the glucocorticoid class of hormones. It is produced in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex within the adrenal gland.

questions.question_text: Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), also called somatomedin C, is a hormone similar in molecular structure to insulin, which plays an important role in childhood growth, and has anabolic effects in adults. From which of the following areas is it secreted?
questions.explanation: Leptin is a hormone predominantly made by adipose cells and enterocytes in the small intestine that helps to regulate energy balance by inhibiting hunger, which in turn diminishes fat storage in adipocytes.

questions.question_text: The Wechsler scale WAIS is a widely used neuropsychological test. Which of the following does it measure?
questions.explanation: IGF-1 is produced primarily by the liver. Production is stimulated by growth hormone (GH). Ref: Laron Z. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1): a growth hormone. Molecular Pathology. 2001 Oct;54(5):311.

questions.question_text: Mr George Francis is a 22-year-old man who has been referred to his local neurology clinic by his GP after collapsing in the street and exhibiting some unusual movements. He is scheduled to have an EEG prior to a clinic appointment. Which of the following is true of EEGs in the investigation of possible seizure disorder?
questions.explanation: The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is an IQ test designed to measure intelligence and cognitive ability in adults and older adolescents. There is an equivalent test for children. Note that there is also a Wechsler's memory scale (WMS).

questions.question_text: Mr Emile Sotoka is a 78 year old man who has presented to his GP with low mood, lack of enjoyment, difficulty focusing on activities and managing his daily tasks and diminished appetite. He has no previous history of significant health disorder. Which of the following would be likely to be identified on a CT scan?
questions.explanation: Epileptiform activity is specific, but not sensitive, for diagnosis of epilepsy as the cause of a transient loss of consciousness or other paroxysmal event that is clinically likely to be epilepsy. EEG has relatively low sensitivity in epilepsy, ranging between 25-56%. Specificity is better, but again variable at 78-98%.

questions.question_text: Cocaine is a relatively common drug of abuse with significant additive potential. Which of the following neurotransmitters explain its effects?
questions.explanation: Elderly patients with depression are more likely to have greater cerebral sulcal atrophy; larger sylvian fissures, lateral ventricles, third ventricles, and temporal horns; and greater severity of subcortical white matter lesions. Depressed patients also exhibit more deep white matter hyperintensities but comparable levels of periventricular hyperintensity to controls. Ref; Salo KI et al. Frontiers in Psychology. 2019;10.

questions.question_text: Mrs Abigail Steuben is a 35-year-old woman with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia who has been taking Clozapine for the past 12 months. She has now reported that she has not had a period for the past 4 months and found that she has a high prolactin level. She is not pregnant. Which of the following investigations would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Cocaine acts by inhibiting the reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine.

questions.question_text: DOPA decarboxylase has an important role in the production of various neurotransmitters. Which of the following molecules is it involved in the synthesis of?
questions.explanation: Clozapine is an uncommon cause of hyperprolactinaemia. Alternative causal factors need to be investigated, particularly the possibility of a pituitary prolactinoma, which is best visualised by MRI.

questions.question_text: The sleep-wake cycle is mediated by a wide range of brain areas. Which of the following areas are not involved in wakefulness?
questions.explanation:
DOPA decarboxylase, also called Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, catalyses several different decarboxylation reactions:
• L-DOPA to dopamine - a neurotransmitter
• L-Phenylalanine to phenethylamine - a trace amine which functions as a neuromodulator
• L-Tyrosine to tyramine - a trace amine neuromodulator
• L-Histidine to histamine - a neurotransmitter
• L-Tryptophan to tryptamine - a trace amine neuromodulator
• 5-HTP to serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) - a neurotransmitter

questions.question_text: The pituitary gland is a key structure for homeostasis and is involved in the synthesis and secretion of a wide variety of hormones. It is divided into anterior, intermediate and posterior lobes. Which of the following is secreted by posterior pituitary lobe?
questions.explanation: A very wide variety of brain regions are associated with the sleep-wake cycle, with multiple interacting neurotransmitter systems in the brain stem, hypothalamus, and basal forebrain converging onto common effector systems in the thalamus and cortex.

questions.question_text: Epigenetics is the study of heritable phenotype changes that do not involve alterations in the DNA sequence. Epigenetics most often involves changes that affect gene activity and expression, but the term can also be used to describe any heritable phenotypic change. Which of the following is not an epigenetic mechanism?
questions.explanation: The posterior pituitary produces: vasopressin (anti-diuretic hormone) and oxytocin. The anterior pituitary produces: growth hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), beta-endorphin, melanocyte-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and prolactin. The intermediate lobe produces melanocyte-stimulating hormone.

questions.question_text: Mr Brian Page is a 28-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. He is currently well and asks his consultant about what causes his symptoms when unwell and how his brain may function differently to other people. Which of the following is most likely to be found in people with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Glycation is the addition of a sugar molecule to a protein without the controlling action of an enzyme. The other mechanisms listed are known epigenetic processes, although there are many others, such as imprinting and alternative splicing.

questions.question_text: Short-term regulation of hunger and food intake involves neural signals from the GI tract, blood levels of nutrients, GI tract hormones, and psychological factors. Which of the following is involved in appetite and satiety?
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia is associated with memory deficits and decreased hippocampal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation.

questions.question_text: The prefrontal cortex is associated with executive functioning, personality, language and planning. Which of the following best represents the percentage of the total brain volume made up by the prefrontal cortex?
questions.explanation: The hormones insulin and cholecystokinin are released from the Gl tract during food absorption and act to suppress feelings of hunger. Cholecystokinin is key in suppressing hunger because of its role in inhibiting neuropeptide Y. Glucagon and adrenaline levels rise during fasting and stimulate hunger. Ghrelin, a hormone produced by the stomach, is a hunger stimulant. Leptin, a hormone produced by adipose tissue, acts as hunger suppressant.

questions.question_text: Early onset Alzheimer's disease is associated with specific genetic variations. If an individual has two copies of the Apo E4 allele, how elevated is their risk of developing Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: The volume of prefrontal cortex white matter relative to total subcortical white matter in the human brain is approximately 12-15%. Ref: Donahue CJ et al. Quantitative assessment of prefrontal cortex in humans relative to nonhuman primates. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2018 May 29;115(22):E5183-92.

questions.question_text: Huntington's disease is a genetic neurodegenerative disorder characterised by early cognitive changes, progressive motor symptoms and eventual dementia. An abnormality in which of the following genes causes it?
questions.explanation: The presence of one Apo E4 allele has been associated with a 2-3 times in the risk of Alzheimer's disease, while the presence of two, is associated with an increase of around 8-15 times (median value of 12x). This varies by study and the effect is not as pronounced in all ethnic groups. (Ref: Williams T, et al. Therapeutic approaches targeting Apolipoprotein E function in Alzheimer's disease. Molecular Neurodegeneration. 2020 Dec 1;15(1):8).

questions.question_text: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease are characterised by particular clinical features and the accumulation of Lewy bodies within the brain. Which of the following molecules are contained within Lewy bodies?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is caused by an abnormally expanded CAG triplets repeat in the Huntingtin gene on the short arm of chromosome 4, at position 4p16.

questions.question_text: Mr Louis Grovener is a 74 year old who has been referred to his local Older Person's Mental Health Service, as he has been experiencing difficulty naming objects and describing what they are for. His family has noticed that he has tended to be more vague in his speech, often saying "thing" or "things" rather than the names of common objects. Which of the following areas is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: A classical Lewy body is an eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion and is primarily composed of alpha-synuclein.

questions.question_text: Mr. Laurence Walden is a 76-year-old man who has been having difficulty finding correct words to use during everyday conversations. He has attended his GP as this has started to significantly impact upon his daily life. His memory appears to be preserved. Which part of his brain is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: This patient is likely to be suffering from semantic dementia or semantic variant primary progressive aphasia. It is one of the frontotemporal dementias. It is characterised by progressive anomia, fluent aphasia, impaired comprehension and visual agnosia in the early stages. This is due to an impairment of semantic memory which stores knowledge and facts. It preferentially affects the temporal lobes, with anterior areas and left lobe tending to show greater atrophy. (Ref: Hodges JR, Patterson K, Oxbury S and Funnell E. Semantic dementia. Progressive fluent aphasia with temporal lobe atrophy. Brain; 1992 December; 115 (6): 1783-1806).

questions.question_text: Dopamine is an important neurotransmitter involved in executive functioning, motor control, motivation and reward. Which of the following dopamine receptors are most abundant in the human brain?
questions.explanation: This scenario describes anomia, which is a form of aphasia characterised by difficulties in word retrieval, with individuals affected being unable to find and use the words they wish to. Similar difficulties can be caused by damage to Broca or Wernicke's area or to the angular gyrus. Anomia can also be a residual aspect of many aphasias, thus localizing it to a single region is considered difficult. But studies using diffusion imaging indicate that lesions affecting the left arcuate fasciculus, a white matter tract, are more likely to cause anomia. (Ref: Anderson JM, Gilmore R, Roper S, et al. Conduction aphasia and the arcuate fasciculus: A reexamination of the Wernicke-Geschwind model. Brain Language; 1999 October;70(1):1-12).

questions.question_text: Which one among the following imaging techniques measures the extent of myelination of white matter fibres at the macroscopic level?
questions.explanation: The D1 receptor is the most abundant dopamine receptor in the brain, followed by D4. D1 receptor is linked to stimulatory G-proteins that activate adenylate cyclase. The D1 receptors are found in high concentration in the substantia nigra pars reticulata, caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, olfactory tubercle, and frontal and temporal cortex. (Ref: Martel JC, Gatti McArthur S. Dopamine Receptor Subtypes, Physiology and Pharmacology: New Ligands and Concepts in Schizophrenia. Frontiers in Pharmacology. 2020; 11:1003. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7379027/).

questions.question_text: ADHD is generally considered to be a lifelong condition that is thought to be heritable. Which of the following genes is associated with ADHD?
questions.explanation: Diffusion tensor imaging measures at the macroscopic level the extent of myelination of white matter fibres using fractional anisotropy, a measure of the degree and directionality of diffusion of water molecules. More recent advances in diffusion tensor imaging include deterministic and global probabilistic tractography, quantitative and more probabilistic measures respectively, of connectivity between reconstructed white matter fibres. Other techniques such as magnetization transfer imaging and quantitative T1 mapping can also be used to quantify the putative myelin content in the brain. (Ref: Palaniyappan L, et al. Aberrant myelination of the cingulum and Schneiderian delusions in schizophrenia: a 7T magnetization transfer study. Psychological medicine. 2019 Aug;49(11):1890-6.)

questions.question_text: Which one among the following imaging technique examines changes in blood oxygen level dependent signal as a proxy measure of neural activity?
questions.explanation: The dopamine receptor D4 (DRD4) and D5 (DRD5) genes have been associated with ADHD. The dopamine transporter gene has also been associated with ADHD previously but evidence has been equivocal. (Ref:Palaniyappan Let al. Reduced Prefrontal Gyrification in Carriers of the Dopamine D4 Receptor 7-Repeat Allele With Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Preliminary Report. Frontiers in Psychiatry. 2019 Apr 25;10:235.).

questions.question_text: Glutamate decarboxylase is an enzyme within the nervous system. It has a role in the synthesis of which of the following neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Functional MRI scan examines changes in blood oxygen level dependent signal (i.e. deoxygenation of haemoglobin) as a proxy measure of neural activity and is used to measure the functional integrity of neural activity.

questions.question_text: GHB (gamma-Hydroxybutyric acid) is medically used as a general anaesthetic, but is also used recreationally. Which of the following receptors does it act on?
questions.explanation: Glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) catalyzes the decarboxylation of glutamate into GABA. GAD has two major isoforms, of 65 and 67 kDa, from two different genes. GAD67 is the major GABA synthesizing form; it is present throughout the soma, in the cytoplasm of inhibitory interneurons. GAD65 is enriched in axon terminals in linkage with synaptic vesicles. Ref: Melzer S, Monyer H. Diversity and function of corticopetal and corticofugal GABAergic projection neurons. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. 2020 Aug 3:1-7.

questions.question_text: There are various types of fronto-temporal dementia characterised by different pathological features. Which of the following is not a form of frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: GHB acts on the specific GHB receptors that are abundant in hippocampal dentate gyrus, median raphe nucleus as well as nucleus accumbens, mediating its effect on memory and sleep but also has weak agonistic action at the GABA-B receptor, mediating addictive properties and GABA-A receptor, mediating anxiolytic and hypnotic effects. Ref: Kamal RM, et al. The neurobiological mechanisms of gamma-hydroxybutyrate dependence and withdrawal and their clinical relevance: a review. Neuropsychobiology. 2016;73(2):65-80.

questions.question_text: Mr. Alan Marston is a 69-year-old man who has recently experienced a cerebrovascular accident. He is frustrated, as he cannot do things as usual. He cannot follow instructions about how to complete a task, such as using a hammer, but can perform each individual step. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease typically affects the basal ganglia in the early phases of the disorder but then generally spreads to affect all cortical areas. Progressive supranuclear palsy was thought to be related to Parkinson's disease, but is now thought to be more related to frontotemporal dementia. (Ref: Finger EC. Frontotemporal Dementias. Continuum (Minneap Minn). 2016;22(2):464-489).

questions.question_text: Pregnancy is associated with numerous physiological changes, which can impact upon the effectiveness of medications. Which of the following occurs in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: This describes ideational apraxia, which occurs when an individual loses the ability to plan movements related to using objects, as they appear to have lost the concept of what the item is for. Ideomotor apraxia is when an individual struggles to imitate or mime movements, such as brushing their hair or teeth. Oculomotor apraxia describes an individual being unable to move their eyes voluntarily; it is seen in Balint's syndrome. Constructional apraxia is when an individual is unable to draw or copy shapes or patterns. Limb-kinetic apraxia is an impairment of co-ordinating voluntary movements of limbs.

questions.question_text: Miss Elaine King is a 35-year-old woman with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. She experiences intermittent auditory hallucinations despite antipsychotic medication. Which of the following would you expect to see on functional imaging when she experiences these hallucinations?

options.text: Reduced activity in the posterior parietal cortex
Increased activity in superior temporal lobe
Reduced activity in the cingulate cortex

correct_answer.text: Increased activity in superior temporal lobe

correct_answers.text: Increased activity in superior temporal lobe

questions.explanation: Pregnancy is associated with a decrease in the production of gastric acid, leading to an increase in overall gastric pH. Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) increases by 50% in the first trimester and continues to increase throughout pregnancy. Gastric emptying and intestinal motility is reduced during pregnancy. Plasma protein binding decreases over the course of pregnancy due to a drop in albumin levels. There are changes in hepatic metabolism of drugs, with some CYP isoforms showing increased activity, with others being less active. There is a marked increase in cardiac output and in the volume of distribution, both in terms of hydrophilic and lipophilic agents. Reference: Johnson-Davis KL, Doyle K. Therapeutic drug monitoring in pregnant patients. Therapeutic Drug Monitoring. 2020 Apr 1;42(2):172-80.

questions.question_text: Noradrenaline is a major neurotransmitter involved in arousal, alertness and anxiety. In which of the following brain areas is noradrenaline produced?
questions.explanation: Noradrenaline is mostly produced in the locus coeruleus ('blue spot').

questions.question_text: Mrs Charlotte Reynolds is a 75-year-old woman who has recently been diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's disease. Which of the following anatomical changes are most likely to be seen on a MRI scan of her brain?
questions.explanation: Medial temporal lobe, and particularly entorhinal, atrophy is considered to be typical of Alzheimer's disease and can be present prior to diagnosis. As the disease progresses, there is progressive neuronal loss across the cortex. (Ref: Jagust W. Imaging the evolution and pathophysiology of Alzheimerdisease. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. 2018 Nov;19(11):687-700.).

questions.question_text: Recreational and therapeutic drugs can impact upon reward pathways in the brain, potentially resulting in dependence or increased reward-seeking behaviour. Which of the following is the reward pathway in the human brain?
questions.explanation: The mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway is recognised as a major reward pathway in the brain, although other areas have a role, such as frontal areas. The mesocortical pathway is more associated with executive functions. The nigrostriatal pathway is associated with movement and associative learning. The tuberoinfundibular pathway is in the hypothalamus and its activation inhibits the release of prolactin. The hypothalamospinal tract influences motor function in the brainstem and spinal cord. (Ref: Maremmani I, Pacini M, Fountoulakis KN. Psychobiology of Addictions. In Psychobiology of Behaviour 2019 (pp. 171-192). Springer.).

questions.question_text: Recent studies on Lewy body dementia suggest hypoperfusion and hypometabolism in which part of the brain areas?
questions.explanation: Single photon emission computerised tomography (SPECT) and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (PET) studies in dementia with Lewy bodies have demonstrated occipital and occipito-parietal visual association area hypoperfusion and hypometabolism respectively. However, occipital deficits are not consistently reported in dementia with Lewy bodies. Higher visual areas, particularly occipito-parietal, appear abnormal in dementia with Lewy bodies, while there is a preservation of function in lower visual areas (V1 and V2/3). (Ref: Ref: Yousaf T, Dervenoulas G, Valkimadi PE and Politis M. Neuroimaging in Lewy body dementia. Journal of Neurology; 2019 Jan;266(1):1-260)

questions.question_text: Mrs. Olive Stanford is an 83-year-old woman who has attended her GP due to worries about her memory. It appears that her functioning is preserved and a MMSE score is normal. Her GP tells her that he feels her difficulties are likely to be part of normal ageing. Which of the following cognitive functions tend to be preserved during ageing?
questions.explanation: Procedural or non-declarative memory functions appear to be well preserved over the lifespan. Semantic memory or knowledge is also relatively preserved compared to episodic memory, although semantic knowledge often has a late life decline. Processing speed tends to decline in later life. (Ref: Lighthall, N. R., Conner, L. B., & Giovanello, K. S. (2019). Learning and memory in the aging brain:The function of declarative and nondeclarative memory over the lifespan. In G. R. Samanez-Larkin (Ed.), The aging brain: Functional adaptation across adulthood (p. 73–109). American Psychological Association.).

questions.question_text: Structural imaging in which of the following types of dementias may reveal midbrain atrophy referred to as the hummingbird sign on sagittal images?
questions.explanation: Structural imaging in PSP may reveal midbrain atrophy referred to as the hummingbird sign on sagittal images. In FDG-PET scans, hypometabolism in frontal, caudate, midbrain, and thalamic regions are notable in PSP. Excerpt from Finger EC. Frontotemporal Dementias. Continuum (Minneap Minn). 2016;22(2):464–489

questions.question_text: Which of the following neurotransmitters is stored in the raphe nuclei?
questions.explanation: Serotonin is produced in large amounts in the neurons originating from the raphe nucleus in the brainstem, with wide-ranging projections to elsewhere in the nervous system. Noradrenaline is associated with the neurons of locus coeruleus in the pons.

questions.question_text: The frontal lobe is associated with a variety of neurological and cognitive functions, in terms of personality, executive functions and speech. Which of the following areas is not a part of the frontal cortex?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area is considered to be located in the temporal lobe, near temporo-parietal junction, on the surface of posterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus. The concept of a secondary motor area is variably described, but the premotor and supplementary motor cortices are located in the frontal lobe.

questions.question_text: The first pass effect is an important element of pharmacokinetics. Which of the following drugs has the least first pass effect?
questions.explanation: The first pass effect is the phenomenon whereby a proportion of an orally administered active drug is metabolised in the liver or gut before it reaches the systemic circulation. Sulpride and amisulpride both have low first pass effects in the liver and gut compared to many other psychotropics. They are extensively eliminated via the renal system. The other medications listed have high first pass effects.

questions.question_text: Antidepressants can have variable effects of sleep, with some being described as activating and others sedating. Which of the following medications is most likely to cause insomnia?
questions.explanation: Duloxetine is associated with insomnia more often than the other medications listed here. SSRIs and venlafaxine are also associated with insomnia, and can be more activating than duloxetine in some cases.

questions.question_text: Sodium valproate is known to increase the risk of congenital malformations if taken by pregnant women. What is the risk of an infant having a major congenital malformation if their mother takes valproate during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Risk for any birth defect quoted 7.2% in Maudsley & NICE. North American registry quotes 10% risk. A large meta-analysis demonstrated that 10.73% of the children of women with epilepsy exposed to valproate monotherapy during pregnancy have congenital malformations. The risk appears to be dose dependent although there is no evidence that there is a dose below which no risk exists. (Ref: DrugSafety Update. MHRA. Medicines related to valproate:risk of abnormal pregnancy outcomes. Available at: www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/medicines-related-to-valproate-risk-of-abnormal-pregnancy-outcomes)

questions.question_text: Sodium valproate is known to increase the risk of developmental delay and other cognitive difficulties in infants if it taken by their mother during pregnancy. What is the risk of this occurring?
questions.explanation: Around 30-40% of children exposed in utero to valproate show delays in early development, including walking and talking. (Ref: Drug Safety Update. MHRA. Medicines related to valproate:risk of abnormal pregnancy outcomes. Available at: www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/medicines-related-to-valproate-risk-of-abnormal-pregnancy-outcomes)

questions.question_text: Tricyclic antidepressants are now used less frequently despite being very effective in treating depression. This is at least partially due to concerns regarding the issue of overdose. Which one of the following tricyclic antidepressants is the most dangerous in overdose?
questions.explanation: Both Amitriptyline and Dosulepin are recognised as being more dangerous in overdose, even when compared to other tricyclic antidepressants. Dosulepin is particularly dangerous and some mental health hospitals have removed it from their formularies.

questions.question_text: Pregabalin is being used more frequently in recent years. Which of the following is true of Pregabalin?

options.text: It passively diffuses across the blood-brain barrier.
It is excreted without being metabolised by the liver
It is effective in treating OCD
It has an exceptionally long half life

correct_answer.text: It is excreted without being metabolised by the liver

correct_answers.text: It is excreted without being metabolised by the liver

questions.explanation: Pregabalin experiences minimal metabolism in the body and is generally excreted unchanged in the urine. Its half-life is around 6 hours. Despite being a GABA analogue, it does not bind to GABA receptors, nor does it modulate GABA transport or metabolism. It is a ligand of certain voltage-dependent calcium channels, which it inhibits. It has low lipophilicity and is transported across the blood-brain barrier by LAT-1. Pregabalin's main indication is for generalised anxiety disorder.

questions.question_text: Miss. Amelie Toutou is a 27-year-old woman with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia. When started on Clozapine she develops symptoms suggestive of myocarditis. Which of the following is a specific indicator of clozapine-induced myocarditis?
questions.explanation: Myocarditis is notoriously difficult to definitively diagnosis, with Troponin and Creatine Kinase levels often showing poor sensitivity for the disorder. In a review conducted of 47 cases of Clozapine induced myocarditis, the development of eosinophilia suggesting IgE mediated hypersensitivity reaction has been documented in ~66% of cases, though interpreting isolated eosinophilia in the absence of other markers is controversial. The Australian treatment guide recommends monitoring for potential myocarditis through baseline and weekly (for the first month) assessments, including vitals, laboratory evaluation of peripheral eosinophils, CRP, ECG, and troponin levels. In the presence of suggestive symptoms of myocarditis, troponin more than twice the upper limit of normal or CRP over 100 mg/L is associated with 100% sensitivity. (Ref: Ronaldson KJ, Taylor AJ, Fitzgerald PB, Topliss DJ, Elsik M, McNeil JJ. Diagnostic characteristics of clozapine-induced myocarditis identified by an analysis of 38 cases and 47 controls. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2010 Aug 1;71(8):976.; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6213891/)

questions.question_text: Mr. Nigel Banks is a 51-year-old man with a history of depression treated with Amitriptyline for 1 year. He stopped taking his medication 3 days ago as he felt his mood has returned to its normal state for several months. Now he reports experiencing tremors, nausea and vomiting. Which of the following is most likely to account for his symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms are most likely the result of abrupt withdrawal of his Amitriptyline. Tricyclic antidepressants can cause significant symptoms as a result of cholinergic rebound after prolonged blockade by the cholinergic receptors.

questions.question_text: Tetrabenazine is a medication used to manage the symptoms of several hyperkinetic movement disorders, including Huntington's Disease, Tourette's Syndrome and Tardive Dyskinesia. Which of the following most accurately describes its mechanism of action?

options.text: Inhibition of acetylcholine receptor muscarinic receptors

questions.explanation: Tetrabenazine depletes monoamines such as dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline and histamine. It appears to achieve this by reversibly inhibiting vesicular monoamine transporter 2, reducing reuptake of monoamines into synaptic vesicles and so diminishing their availability.

questions.question_text: Antidepressants usually affect the function of serotonin and noradrenaline to produce their therapeutic effects. Which of the following antidepressants has the most effect on dopamine levels?
questions.explanation: The pharmacological properties of SNRIs such as duloxetine depend on their dose. Serotonergic reuptake inhibition predominates at low doses, while additional NE reuptake inhibition occurs at medium doses. At higher doses, they weakly inhibit dopamine reuptake. Recent evidence indicates that NE transporter also transports some dopamine in the prefrontal cortex. The prefrontal cortex has low concentration of dopamine reuptake transporters (DAT); therefore, SNRIs such as duloxetine can substantially increase dopaminergic neurotransmission in prefrontal cortex. Ref: Carboni, E., Tanda, G. L., Frau, R., and Di Chiara, G. (1990). Blockade of the noradrenaline carrier increases extracellular dopamine concentrations in the prefrontal cortex: evidence that dopamine is taken up in vivo by noradrenergic terminals. J. Neurochem. 55, 1067–1070.

questions.question_text: Donepezil is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor often used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. Which of the following hepatic enzyme metabolizes Donepezil?
questions.explanation: Donepezil is broken down into 4 metabolites, 2 of which are active. It is metabolised by CYP 450 isoenzymes 2D6 as well as 3A4.

questions.question_text: Mr. Daniel Lightfoot is a 32-year-old man with a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder for which he has been taking Lithium for the past 5 years. He now reports feeling the urge to drink more water than usual and is urinating a large amount. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Lithium accumulates in the cells of the collecting duct of the nephrons and inhibits ADH's ability to increase water permeability. Thus, chronic lithium use affects the nephron's ability to respond to ADH. This ADH-resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) results in polydipsia and polyuria, affecting ~40% of patients on long-term lithium therapy Ref: Ellingrod VL. Lithium-induced diabetes insipidus: Prevention and management. Current Psychiatry. 2013 Jul;12(7):42-5.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Emma Premack is a 61-year-old woman who has Type II diabetes mellitus and has unfortunately developed significant pain due to peripheral neuropathy and is presenting with notable depression. Which of the following medications would be most helpful for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Duloxetine is licensed as an antidepressant and also for the treatment of peripheral nerve pain and urinary incontinence.

questions.question_text: Cytochrome 450 1A2 is an important enzyme in the metabolism of a variety of medications. Which of the following induces its production?
questions.explanation: Smoking cigarettes, taking modafinil or omeprazole can induce CYP450 1A2 production. The other options presented inhibit this enzyme to variable degree.

questions.question_text: Antidepressants can be associated with a withdrawal syndrome when they are stopped or the dose is reduced. Which of the following drugs when stopped suddenly is most likely to be associated with withdrawal symptoms?
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine and paroxetine are associated with significant withdrawal syndromes and should be reduced and discontinued with caution.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants is least likely to cause hypotension?
questions.explanation: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is relatively common with Mirtazapine and Trazodone. It is also linked to tricyclic antidepressants and older monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Postural hypotension can occur with SSRIs and SNRIs, but is less common.

questions.question_text: Mr. Alan Mitchell is a 63-year-old man with a history of depression and cardiac failure for which he takes Furosemide and Ramipril. He presents to his GP with leg cramps, progressive weakness and constipation. An ECG in the surgery demonstrated T wave flattening. Which of the following electrolyte imbalances is most likely to account for his symptoms?
questions.explanation: T wave flattening is characteristic of hypokalaemia. It often presents with non-specific leg cramps and weakness before progressing to paresis and a variety of renal, cardiac, neurological and gastrointestinal disturbances.

questions.question_text: Benzodiazepines are often used in clinical practice as short-term sedatives and hypnotics. Which of the following best describes their mechanism of action?

options.text: Decreases neuronal excitability via GABAA receptor
Decreases neuronal excitability via GABAB receptor
Increases neuronal excitability via GABAA receptor
Increases neuronal excitability via GABAB receptor
Increases neuronal excitability via GABAC receptor

correct_answer.text: Decreases neuronal excitability via GABAA receptor

correct_answers.text: Decreases neuronal excitability via GABAA receptor

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines increase the efficiency of GABA by hyperpolarising the cell membrane of neurons after attaching to the GABAA receptor subtype between the α and γ subunits. This decreases the excitability of the neuron and so the brain overall.

questions.question_text: Miss Annunziata Farage is a 25-year-old woman who has been brought to her local A&E after collapsing and making odd movements in the street. The medical staff are querying whether the episode was epileptic in nature or if it was psychologically driven. Which of the following would be most specific for differentiating between epileptic and pseudo seizures in this case?
questions.explanation: Prolactin levels taken 10-20 minutes after a possible seizure are highly specific (around 96%) for identifying epileptic seizures. (Ref: Chen DK, So YT, Fisher RS. Use of serum prolactin in diagnosing epileptic seizures: report of the Therapeutics and Technology Assessment Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology. Neurology; 2005 Sep 13;65(5):668-75).

questions.question_text: Mrs. Ivy Richards is a 76-year-old woman who is due to be started on memantine. Her daughter has some queries about its action and use. Which of the following is not true regarding memantine?

options.text: It can cause bradycardia as a side-effect
It is indicated in moderate to severe vascular dementia
It potentiates the effect of Acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors.
It is an antagonist at NMDA receptors

correct_answer.text: It can cause bradycardia as a side-effect

correct_answers.text: It can cause bradycardia as a side-effect

questions.explanation: Memantine is a NMDA antagonist used in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. Its half-life is 60-80 hours. Common side effects are hallucinations and confusion. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, not memantine, are associated with bradycardia.

questions.question_text: Mr Evan Stevens is a 32-year-old man with a history of treatment resistant schizophrenia who will be started on clozapine in the next few weeks. When he attended the clozapine clinic for an information session, he was advised about the effect of smoking on Clozapine. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in smokers on clozapine?
questions.explanation: Smoking stimulates CYP450 1A2, which metabolises clozapine. This results in lower serum levels.

questions.question_text: Ingested psychotropic medications are metabolised in a variety of ways. Which of the following drugs follows zero order kinetics?
questions.explanation: In zero order kinetics, a constant amount, rather than percentage, of the drug is eliminated per unit of time even when therapeutic doses are taken, e.g. a fixed 1 mg per hour. This is independent of the concentration of the drug in the serum. Examples of drugs following zero order kinetics are phenytoin, aspirin and ethanol.

questions.question_text: Lithium's efficacy depends upon it remaining within a therapeutic window in terms of serum level. Its serum level can be significantly affected by certain medications. Which of the following drugs reduces serum lithium levels?
questions.explanation: Drugs that reduce lithium levels include theophylline, caffeine, and acetazolamide. Additionally, increasing dietary sodium intake may also reduce lithium levels by prompting the kidneys to excrete more lithium. Furosemide, thiazides, ibuprofen and ACE inhibitors tend to increase lithium levels. Tramadol and certain other opiates can precipitate serotonin syndrome in association with lithium. Haloperidol and other antipsychotics can increase the risk of toxic encephalopathy, without affecting lithium levels.

questions.question_text: Agomelatine is a relatively new antidepressant, which binds to melatonin receptors where it acts as an agonist. Which of the following other receptors does agomelatine bind to?
questions.explanation: Agomelatine is a potent agonist at melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors and an antagonist at 5-HT2C receptors. The psychotropic effects of agomelatine are likely related to both melatonergic and 5-HT effects. (Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20946699)

questions.question_text: Social anxiety is characterised by avoidance of and anxiety over social situations where an individual will be observed by others. Which of the following drugs has proven effective for social anxiety?
questions.explanation: Some research has found Pregabalin to be effective in the treatment of social anxiety. Pregabalin 600 mg/day was an effective and well-tolerated treatment of social anxiety disorder. Somnolence and dizziness were the most frequently reported adverse events. Please note that pregabalin is not endorsed by NICE which instead recommends SSRIs, Venlafaxine and MAOIs, particularly moclobemide. (Ref: Pande AC et al. Efficacy of the novel anxiolytic pregabalin in social anxiety disorder: a placebo-controlled, multicenter study. Journal Clinical Psychopharmacology, 2004 Apr; 2:141-9).

questions.question_text: The CATIE study showed what percentage risk of metabolic syndrome in patients with schizophrenia receiving antipsychotic treatment?
questions.explanation: The prevalence of metabolic syndrome in CATIE cohort was 40.9% and 42.7%, respectively using the NCEP and AHA derived criteria. In females it was 51.6% and 54.2% using the NCEP and AHA criteria, compared to 36.0% (p = .0002) and 36.6% (p = .0003), respectively for males. Ref; McEvoy JP, et al. Schizophrenia research. 2005 Dec 1;80(1):19-32.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a prodrug?
questions.explanation: A prodrug is a medication or compound that, after administration, is metabolised into a pharmacologically active drug. Desipramine is the metabolite of imipramine. All the others listed above are pro-drugs.

questions.question_text: Mr Nicholas Orgreave is a 31-year-old man with a history of paranoid schizophrenia who has recently been started on a Haloperidol depot after being admitted following a relapse due to medication non-compliance in the community. He becomes agitated on the ward in response to auditory hallucinations and the ward staff request advice around tranquilisation. Which of the following would be most appropriate to give him as a first-line option?
questions.explanation: Second generation antipsychotics are generally preferred in the treatment of agitation related to psychotic illness. Benzodiazepines can be effective in sedating a patient but do not address the underlying drivers for the behaviour i.e. psychosis in this case.

questions.question_text: What is the annual risk of developing tardive dyskinesia in individuals in individual exposed to long-term typical antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia is a disorder that results in involuntary, repetitive body movements. This may include grimacing, sticking out the tongue, or smacking the lips. It is associated with long-term antipsychotic use. Long term use of typical antipsychotics, such as Haloperidol, are associated with a risk of around 25-30% of developing tardive dyskinesia, at a rate of 5% of patients per year of antipsychotic exposure. Nearly 50% of these cases are reversible. Ref: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines 13th edition. Also see Caligiuri M. Tardive dyskinesia: a task force report of the American Psychiatric Association. Hosp Community Psychiatry 1993; 44:190.

questions.question_text: Mr Adrian Dawes is a 48-year-old man who is experiencing a significant depressive episode with marked difficulty getting to sleep and then waking frequently in the night. He is finding this exhausting and has asked about medication that might help him get to and stay asleep. Which of the following would be most appropriate for him?
questions.explanation: Temazepam is recommended as a medication to aid the initiation and maintenance of sleep. It has a mean half-life of around 8 hours, although the range can be 8-20 hours. This usually limits early morning tiredness.

questions.question_text: Mr Ian Watkins is a 37-year-old man with a long-standing history of bipolar affective disorder that has not responded well to medication trials. He has read about Topiramate as a potential treatment option and would want to know more about it. Which of the following is a common side effect of Topiramate?
questions.explanation: Weight loss is a common side effect of Topiramate.

questions.question_text: Lithium is a very effective mood stabiliser but needs to be maintained within a therapeutic range, with a risk of toxicity if the serum level is too high. Which of the following is most likely to make lithium toxicity worse?
questions.explanation: Furosemide significantly increases the serum level of Lithium and can also increase the risk of hypokalaemia and torsades de pointes. Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs can increase the serum Lithium level although the risk varies within the drug class. Prednisolone can increase the risk of hypokalaemia. Theophylline can decrease the level of Lithium.

questions.question_text: GHB (γ-Hydroxybutyric acid) is a naturally occurring neurotransmitter and a psychoactive drug. It is a precursor to GABA, glutamate, and glycine in certain brain areas. Which of the following receptors does it work on?
questions.explanation: GHB functions at both the GABA-B receptor but also at the γ-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) receptor (GHBR), which is G-protein-coupled. GHBR is also a transporter for riboflavin. Ref: Crunelli V, Emri Z, Leresche N. Unravelling the brain targets of γ-hydroxybutyric acid. Current opinion in pharmacology. 2006 Feb 1;6(1):44-52.

questions.question_text: Diazepam is a commonly used medication. Which of the following receptors does it act on?
questions.explanation: Diazepam binds to the GABA-A receptors, which are ligand-gated chloride-selective ion channels, which are activated by GABA. Diazepam and other benzodiazepines enhance the binding of GABA, which leads to an increase in chloride within the neuron that causes hyperpolarization. This makes neuronal excitation more difficult and reduces the likelihood of neuronal firing.

questions.question_text: New medications must undergo testing prior to being approved for general use to ensure their efficacy and safety. How many stages of approval must a medication pass through prior to general use?
questions.explanation: There are 6 stages of clinical trials related to a new medication, with the last stage (phase 4) comes after general use begins (post-marketing). The stages are: Preclinical - Animal or in vitro studies to determine toxicity, pharmacokinetics and initial indications of efficacy. Phase 0 - Small sample of human subjects exposed to low dose to further investigate pharmacokinetics. Phase 1 - Larger sample of healthy volunteers with increasing doses used to determine appropriate ranges. Phase 2 - Testing on group of patients to determine efficacy in clinical practice Phase 3 - Testing on larger group of patients to establish efficacy, effectiveness and safety Phase 4 - Post-marketing monitoring after the medication is released for general use.

questions.question_text: Mr Johnson Nash is a 57-year-old man with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia who has been well on the same medication for several years. Unfortunately he has now developed autoimmune hepatitis, which his hepatology team is struggling to manage. There are concerns about whether he can continue on his current medication regime for schizophrenia. Which of the following antipsychotics are most appropriate for individuals with significant hepatic impairment?
questions.explanation: Amisulpride and Sulpiride are predominantly renally excreted and both are safer antipsychotic medicines that could be used in patients with hepatic impairmemt. (Ref: Telles-Correia D, et al. Psychotropic drugs and liver disease: A critical review of pharmacokinetics and liver toxicity. World Journal of Gastrointestinal Pharmacology and Therapeutics. 2017;8(1):26Å38)

questions.question_text: Which of the following SSRIs has an active metabolite?
questions.explanation: Sertraline also has an active metabolite, N-desmethyl sertraline, which is 10 times less potent than sertraline itself. Fluoxetine also has an active metabolite norfluoxetine with a long half-life.

questions.question_text: Miss Janet Baldwin is a 24-year-old woman with a new diagnosis of first episode psychosis. She has a history of recurrent hypotension without an established cause and is keen that any medication does not worsen this. Which of the following antipsychotics is least likely to cause hypotension?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole is associated with a low risk of postural hypotension compared to other antipsychotics. It is thought to be linked to antagonism of alpha-1-adrenergic receptors which are associated with vasoconstriction. (Ref: Polcwiartek C, et al. Cardiovascular safety of antipsychotics: a clinical overview, Expert Opinion on Drug Safety; 2016;15:5:679-688).

questions.question_text: The half-lives of psychiatric medications vary widely and this can influence the time necessary for them to reach steady state. Which of the following medications has a half-life of more than 50 hours if taken orally?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole has a half-life of around 75 hours. Flupentixol and Citalopram have half-lives of around 35 hours. Venlafaxine has a half-life of 3 to 7 hours, while its active metabolite, desvenlafaxine, has a half-life of 9 to 13 hours. Mirtazapine has a half-life of 20-40 hours.

questions.question_text: Many psychotropic medications can reduce the seizure threshold as a side-effect. Which of the following antipsychotics is associated with the highest risk of seizures?
questions.explanation: Clozapine is the highest risk antipsychotic for seizures, with a cumulative risk 10% for seizure activity. Chlorpromazine is the highest risk first generation antipsychotic for seizures. (Ref: Bhatti M, Dorriz P and Mehndiratta P. Impact of Psychotropic drugs on Seizure threshold. Neurology;2017 April;88(16 Supplement).

questions.question_text: MAOI antidepressants have been largely replaced by other agents due to concerns around significant interactions with other medications and foods. Which of the following should not be used concurrently with a MAOI?
questions.explanation: MAOIs have been associated with hypertensive crises when used with over the counter decongestants. (Ref: Carlo AD, Alpert JE. Catastrophic Drug-Drug Interactions in Psychopharmacology. Psychiatric Annals. 2016 Aug 12;46(8):439-47.

questions.question_text: Medications within the same class can have widely ranging half-lives, which can influence their potential for adverse effects and dosing regimes. Which of the following SSRI antidepressants has the shortest half-life?
questions.explanation: Fluvoxamine is thought to have a half-life of around 16 hours. The half-lives of other SSRIs are Paroxetine - 21 hours, Sertraline - 26 hours, Citalopram - 35 hours, Fluoxetine - 1-4 days (Norfluoxetine - 7-9 days). (Ref: Marazziti D, Avella MT, Basile L, Mucci F, Dell'Osso L. Pharmacokinetics of serotonergic drugs: focus on OCD. Expert Opinion on Drug Metabolism & Toxicology. 2019 Apr 3;15(4):261-73).

questions.question_text: Lurasidone is a relatively new antipsychotic medication. Which of the following is true regarding its absorption?
questions.explanation: Lurasidone is weakly soluble in water; its bioavailability is limited after regular oral ingestion. When administered with a meal of at least 350 calories, the bioavailability increases by 2-3 times. (Ref: Jaeschke RR, et al. Lurasidone: The 2016 update on the pharmacology, efficacy and safety profile. Pharmacological Reports. 2016 Jul 1;68(4):748-55.).

questions.question_text: Zolpidem is a commonly used hypnotic medication that has a shorter half-life than Zopiclone. Which of the following receptors does it act upon?
questions.explanation: Zolpidem acts at the GABA-A receptor benzodiazepine site; but unlike benzodiazepines that non-selectively bind to all GABA-A receptor subtypes, zolpidem exhibits preferential binding with a high affinity for the alpha1 subunit, with lower affinity for alpha2/3 subunits. Its sedative effects (and anti-convulsant properties in vitro) are derived exclusively from its action on the alpha1 subunit. (Ref: Neumann E, et al. Zolpidem Activation of Alpha 1-Containing GABAA Receptors Selectively Inhibits High Frequency Action Potential Firing of Cortical Neurons. Front Pharmacol. 2018;9:1523.).

questions.question_text: Miss Jane Sessions is a 28-year-old woman with a diagnosis of first episode psychosis. She has agreed to start an antipsychotic but is worried as she has heard that they are associated with weight gain. By which of the following mechanisms can antipsychotics lead to an increase in weight?
questions.explanation: Weight gain associated with antipsychotics is thought to be linked to multiple mechanisms, including antagonism at H1 receptors, which increases appetite by impairing hypothalamic functioning and falsely indicating negative energy balance. It is also associated with 5HT2C antagonism, which delays the onset of satiety, and 5HT1A agonism, increasing food intake. Interesting, dopamine blockade may also increase weight by impairing limbic systems and leading to more reward-seeking behaviour, such as eating. (Ref: He M, et al. The role of hypothalamic H1 receptor antagonism in antipsychotic-induced weight gain. CNS drugs. 2013 Jun 1;27(6):423-34).

questions.question_text: Old age is associated with significant physiological changes that impact upon the effectiveness and tolerance of medications. With respect to drug distribution, which of the following tends to occur with normal aging?

options.text: Increase in lipophilic drug distribution and decrease in hydrophilic drug distribution
Increase in both lipophilic and hydrophilic drug distribution
Decrease in both hydrophilic and lipophilic drug distribution.
Decrease in hydrophilic drug distribution and no change in lipophilic drug distribution
Increase is hydrophilic drug distribution and decrease in lipophilic drug distribution

correct_answer.text: Increase in lipophilic drug distribution and decrease in hydrophilic drug distribution

correct_answers.text: Increase in lipophilic drug distribution and decrease in hydrophilic drug distribution

questions.explanation: Older people tend to have a higher volume of distribution for lipophilic drugs and a lower one for hydrophilic medications. They tend to have reduced effectiveness of first pass hepatic metabolism and CYP isoform activity. Renal clearance is often reduced. (Ref: Reeve E, Trenaman SC, Rockwood K, Hilmer SN. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic alterations in older people with dementia. Expert opinion on drug metabolism & toxicology. 2017 Jun 3;13(6):651-68).

questions.question_text: Pregabalin is an antiepileptic medication that is also used in chronic pain and anxiety. Which of the following is true regarding this medication?

options.text: It has no association with weight gain
It is excreted without being metabolized
It is an agonist of calcium channels

correct_answer.text: It is excreted without being metabolized

correct_answers.text: It is excreted without being metabolized

questions.explanation: Pregabalin undergoes very little metabolism and around 98% is unchanged and excreted renally. It has good oral bioavailability. Its half-life is around 6-11 hours so is usually administered 2-3 times per day. It is an inhibitor of certain calcium channels. It is associated with some increase in weight. Ref: Chincholkar M. Gabapentinoids: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and considerations for clinical practice. British Journal of Pain. 2020 May;14(2):104-14

questions.question_text: Miss Susan Stolet is a 24-year-old woman who has recently been diagnosed with epilepsy and started on an anticonvulsant. She returns to clinic with her mother who has noticed that her behaviour has changed and become more aggressive since the medication was started. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Levetiracetam is associated with a high rate of behavioural side-effects, with one study suggesting that 13% of patients may experience this. Topiramate is also associated with a high rate of behavioural and aggressive side-effects, although this can be associated with reduced seizure control, which may indicate it is partially an ictal phenomenon. (Ref: Brodie MJ, Besag F, Ettinger AB, et al. Epilepsy, Antiepileptic Drugs, and Aggression: An Evidence-Based Review. Pharmacology Review; 2016;68(3):563–602).

questions.question_text: A GP has started a psychiatric patient on Ramipril for treatment of his hypertension. The GP is worried about drug interactions as he is on a number of psychiatric medicines. Which of the following drugs can have elevated levels if prescribed with Ramipril?
questions.explanation: Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor. Lithium is known to have significant drug interactions with medications that affect kidney tubule functioning, including NSAIDs, diuretics and ACE inhibitors. These medications generally result in a significant increase in serum Lithium levels and can lead to toxicity.(Ref: Hommers L, et al. The combination of lithium and ACE inhibitors: Hazardous, critical, possible?. Clinical drug investigation. 2019 May 1;39(5):485-90).

questions.question_text: Protein binding of medications can have a significant effect upon their efficacy and metabolism. Which of the following antidepressants is most highly protein bound?
questions.explanation: Sertraline is 98% protein bound. The percentages for other SSRIs are Citalopram - 80%, Escitalopram - 56%, Fluoxetine - 95% and Paroxetine - 93-95% (Ref: Ciraulo, DA; Shader, RI, eds. (2011). Pharmacotherapy of Depression. SpringerLink (2nd ed.). New York, NY: Humana Press).

questions.question_text: Antidepressants can be associated with QTc prolongation and potential torsades de pointes. Which of the following antidepressants is least associated with QTc prolongation?
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine, Sertraline and Reboxetine are least associated with QTc prolongation at therapeutic doses. Tricyclics are best avoided completely in patients at risk of serious arrhythmias. Citalopram, Moclobemide and venlafaxine should be used with caution or avoided in those at risk of serious arrhythmias. (Ref: Rochester MP, et al. Evaluating the risk of QTc prolongation associated with antidepressant use in older adults: a review of the evidence. Therapeutic advances in drug safety. 2018 Jun;9(6):297-308.).

questions.question_text: Mr. Thomas Eaton is a 25-year-old man with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia and depression. He has recently been started on haloperidol and paroxetine but is brought into his local A&E by his family after developing a fever and jerking in his limbs. In hospital, it is found that his pulse and blood pressure are elevated and he is demonstrating clonus. Which of the following is he most likely to be experiencing?
questions.explanation: This is most likely to represent serotonin syndrome, which is characterised by elevated bodily temperature, hypertension, tachycardia, dilated pupils, myoclonus, clonus and agitation. It tends to be acute in onset. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome can present with similar symptoms but is less acute in onset and is not associated with myoclonus or clonus.

questions.question_text: John is a 59-year-old man taking psychotropic medications for a long time. He has recently been diagnosed with interstitial nephritis. Which of the following can cause this adverse reaction?
questions.explanation: Long term Lithium use is associated with chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy, which is characterised by declining GFR without marked proteinuria. It is also associated with long-term thyroid and parathyroid dysfunction. (Ref: Kovvuru K, Kanduri SR, Thongprayoon C, Cheungpasitporn W.Lithium and nephrotoxicity: Nephrology's perspectives. Bipolar Disorders. 2020 Jun;22(4):331-3.).

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications acts as a D2 receptor agonist?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole acts as a partial agonist at D2 receptors making it unique amongst antipsychotic medications. None of the other listed medications have agonistic actions at D2. The correct answer is: Aripiprazole
